name: RPC INC

priced.reason: not a repriceable fcff name or no growth supplied

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: That the verdict recorded three weeks ago was `rich` on this same business, the fundamentals have not improved, and changing to `no_edge` purely because the stock fell 19% is the market talking me out of a view rather than evidence doing it. On the prior pass's own arithmetic — a $78M sustaining base, zero growth, a defensible 12.7% cost of equity from a 1.4 oilfield-services beta — fair value is $3.89, and at $5.06 the stock is still 23% above it. The red team's job is to hold the earlier verdict to its stated test, and that test was failed by a factor of fifty and failed again: nine-month free cash flow of $5.0M against a base of $132.3M.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Whether the sign of the answer is robust across the discount rates I can defend. If every cell at a defensible growth rate stays negative, `rich` holds; if the sign flips inside the band, the verdict is the band and not the point.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Yes, and this is where the counter loses and the verdict changes. At the corrected $78M base the market now requires -1.0% five-year FCFF growth at the engine's 9.40% cost of equity, +3.6% at 11.0%, +8.0% at 12.70% and +10.6% at 13.80%. The fair-value grid at zero growth reads $5.25 (+3.8%), $4.47 (-11.7%), $3.89 (-23.1%) and $3.61 (-28.7%). At $6.28 three weeks ago every one of those cells was negative, which is what made `rich` right then; at $5.06 the top cell has crossed zero. So the sign of the answer is now set by the beta — and the beta is 0.80 at an R-squared of 0.094, a failed regression on a Permian pressure pumper, which is precisely the input this file says must not decide a verdict and which the schema has no field to override. Two large uncertainties pointing opposite ways — a trough base that could be too low if 2026 is the bottom, and a cost of equity that is certainly too low — is the SM condition, and the answer is the range, not the average. The counter is right that the business has not improved; it is wrong that the verdict can stand, because the verdict was never about the business alone.
devils_advocate.unresolved: Whether 2026 is the cycle bottom — the whole question, and unchanged from the last pass: at trough earning power the name is rich and at mid-cycle it is cheap. Also unresolved: what Saltiel will do with the net cash, which is now a material swing factor the last pass did not have to consider, and whether a new CEO's first act is a write-down or a purchase. And I still have no disclosed maintenance-versus-growth capex split; the capex-below-D&A inference is strong but it is an inference, and the 10-Q confirms the split exists internally without publishing it.

what_changed: A complete leadership transition, announced after most of the 21-day fall. On 2026-11-18 RPC appointed Rob Saltiel President and CEO and a director effective 2026-11-20 — a three-time public-company CEO (MRC Global 2021 through its 2025 merger with DNOW, Key Energy Services, Atwood Oceanics, senior roles at Transocean) succeeding Ben Palmer, whose retirement was announced in June 2026. On 2026-11-11 Executive Chairman Richard Hubbell, forty years with RPC and CEO from 2003 to 2022, notified the company of his retirement effective 2026-12-31, contingent on a new CEO being appointed, and will serve as Special Advisor through 2027-03-31. Lead Independent Director Patrick Gunning becomes NON-EXECUTIVE Chairman from 2027-01-01. Gunning's own framing is that 'RPC has the portfolio and financial flexibility to pursue meaningful growth as the market improves.' So an owner-operator board with an executive chairman has been replaced by an outside professional CEO with an M&A and margin record, and an independent chair, at a company holding $177M of net cash. None of the five observables the 2026-10-30 pass nominated has reported — there has been no Q4 print, no 2027 capital budget and no new impairment since the 2026-10-29 10-Q.
consensus_case: At $5.06, after a 19.3% fall in 21 days against an Energy sector median of -7.4%, the market is paying about $944M of enterprise value for a debt-free pressure pumper with $177M of cash, roughly $263M of annualised adjusted EBITDA, and a brand-new chief executive hired explicitly to pursue growth. The bear owns the near term: US pressure pumping is structurally oversupplied, management will not reactivate frac fleets at current pricing, nine-month free cash flow was $5.0M, and the one acquisition that created the apparent growth has been impaired. The price now embeds that: at the engine's own 9.4% cost of equity the market requires only -1.0% five-year FCFF growth off a sustaining base of $78M, which is a liquidation assumption for a franchise with leading-edge completions technology and no debt.
base_case_rationale: I keep the prior pass's sustaining base of roughly $78M, built from ~$263M of annualised adjusted EBITDA less $148-170M of sustaining capital expenditure, taxed, and I keep zero growth paired with it under the AROC rule. The 10-Q of 2026-10-29 re-confirms the test that settles the maintenance-versus-growth question against the owner: capex of $148.4M in the newest year sits BELOW depreciation and amortisation of $161.2M, and annualised 2026 capex of about $148M sits below roughly $170M of D&A. A company not out-spending its own depreciation has no material growth-capex add-back available, so the near-zero reported free cash flow is close to honest owner earnings and the engine's $132.3M three-year mean — which spans a 2022-23 activity spike and whose oldest year is $213.8M — is roughly 1.7x current earning power. What has changed is not the base but the price, and the price is now low enough that the base no longer settles the verdict.
key_risks: The 8.3-9.4% cost of equity rests on a beta of 0.80 at an R-squared of 0.094 for a 100%-equity-funded Permian pressure pumper; it alone decides the sign, and the schema cannot override it
Nine-month 2026 free cash flow of $5.0M against an engine base of $132.3M, with capex below depreciation removing the growth-capex defence
US pressure pumping is structurally oversupplied; management will not reactivate frac fleets at current pricing
Pintail impaired $74.5M in Q3 2026 on management's own DCF; further impairments named as possible
A new CEO with a growth mandate and $177M of net cash is a capital-allocation risk as well as an opportunity
The +279.7% headline gap rests on a +22.1% five-year revenue CAGR that is largely the ~$245M Pintail purchase of April 2025 — acquired revenue applied to per-share free cash flow
watch_for: Q4 2026 free cash flow above roughly $50M, which would lift the full-year base toward $100M — the prior pass's test, still unreported
2027 capital expenditure guided below ~$130M, clearly beneath ~$170M of depreciation — the only thing that would prove a material part of 2026 spend was growth
Saltiel's first capital-allocation decision: an acquisition, a buyback, or a special dividend from the $177M of net cash
A fourth consecutive quarter of adjusted EBITDA expansion above ~$75M
Any announcement that RPC is reactivating frac fleets — management's own stated threshold for pricing having cleared
